---
title: "Selectors: asking for collections"
---

So far you have asked the page for one element at a time. `querySelector`
returns the first match and stops looking. A real page has twelve list items
and forty links, and the first one is rarely the one you want. This chapter is
about asking for all of them at once.

## Five paragraphs, one loop {#sec-selectors-experiment}

Create a new app from our template and replace everything inside `<body>` with
this:

```html
<h1>Five paragraphs</h1>
<p>One</p>
<p>Two</p>
<p>Three</p>
<p>Four</p>
<p>Five</p>
<script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
```

Then replace the content of `src/index.ts` with this:

```ts
const paragraphs = document.querySelectorAll('p');

for (const paragraph of paragraphs) {
  paragraph.style.color = 'teal';
}
```

Run `npm start`. All five paragraphs turn teal. You wrote the pattern `p`
once and reached every paragraph on the page.

Now get the same result with no TypeScript at all. Create `src/styles.css`:

```css
p {
  color: teal;
}
```

Add `import './styles.css';` as the first line of `src/index.ts`, then delete
the `querySelectorAll` line and the loop. Reload the page. The paragraphs are
still teal.

## One selector language, two users {#sec-selectors-two-users}

The pattern `p` did the same job twice. In the stylesheet it decided which
elements the rule paints. In TypeScript it decided which elements came back
from the document. A **selector** is a pattern that describes elements, and
the browser reads it the same way in both places.

That halves your work for the rest of the year. Every selector you pick up for
styling also works in `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll`, and every
selector you pick up for code also works in a stylesheet.

So which of the two should do a job? When the look never changes, let the
stylesheet do it and keep your TypeScript short. When the look changes because
something happened, let TypeScript add or remove a class and let the
stylesheet hold the colors. That is the `classList` trick from the to-do list,
and now you can see why it works: both sides speak about the same class name.

## The selector kinds you need now {#sec-selectors-kinds}

Every example below talks about this markup:

```html
<ul id="shoppingList">
  <li class="done">Milk</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li class="done">Apples</li>
</ul>
<input id="newItem" type="text">
<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">MDN</a>
```

**A tag name** matches every element with that tag.

```css
li {
  padding: 0.2rem;
}
```

```ts
const items = document.querySelectorAll('li');
```

**A class** starts with a dot and matches every element that carries it, so
`.done` finds Milk and Apples.

```css
.done {
  color: gray;
}
```

```ts
const finished = document.querySelectorAll('.done');
```

**An id** starts with a hash and matches the single element that has it.

```css
#newItem {
  width: 12rem;
}
```

```ts
const input = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#newItem');
```

**Two conditions on one element** are written with nothing between them.
`li.done` means an `li` that also has the class `done`.

**A space means "inside"**. `#shoppingList li` matches every `li` somewhere
inside the list, however deeply it is nested.

```css
#shoppingList li {
  cursor: pointer;
}
```

```ts
const listItems = document.querySelectorAll('#shoppingList li');
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## One space, two different answers

`ul .done` with a space matches elements with class `done` that sit inside a
`ul`. `ul.done` without a space matches a `ul` that carries the class itself.
The browser reports no error either way, so a missing space shows up as an
empty page instead of a message.
:::

**A position** is written after a colon. `li:first-child` matches Milk, and
`li:nth-child(odd)` matches Milk and Apples, the first and the third.

```css
#shoppingList li:nth-child(odd) {
  background-color: #eee;
}
```

```ts
const oddItems = document.querySelectorAll('#shoppingList li:nth-child(odd)');
```

**The mouse pointer** uses a colon too. `li:hover` matches the item the
pointer is on right now.

```css
li:hover {
  background-color: gold;
}
```

You can hand `li:hover` to `querySelectorAll` as well and get whatever sits
under the pointer at that moment, but that is rarely useful. Leave `:hover` in
the stylesheet, where the browser keeps it correct for free.

**An attribute** goes in square brackets. `input[type="text"]` matches text
inputs and ignores checkboxes. Write `^=` in place of `=` and only the start
of the value has to match, so `a[href^="https://"]` picks the links that leave
your own site.

```css
a[href^="https://"] {
  color: purple;
}
```

```ts
const externalLinks = document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="https://"]');
```

There are many more kinds. When you need one, MDN's
[CSS selectors reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_selectors)
lists them with examples, and your coding buddy explains any selector you meet
in someone else's code.

## One object, or a collection of them {#sec-selectors-collection}

`querySelector` answers with one element or with `null`, which is why you
check the result before you use it. `querySelectorAll` answers with a
collection of elements. When nothing matches you get an empty collection
instead of `null`, so there is no null check here. `.length` tells you how
many elements came back:

```ts
const finished = document.querySelectorAll('.done');
console.log(`${finished.length} items are done`);
```

At the start of this part you met the first idea of object-oriented
programming: an element on the page is an object with properties you can read
and write. Here is the second one. Objects come in collections. You ask the
document once and get many objects back, and a single loop then treats every
one of them the same way:

```ts
for (const item of finished) {
  item.classList.remove('done');
}
```

Nearly every program in the rest of this book has that shape. Ask for a
collection, loop over it, change each object.

When you need a property that only one kind of element has, such as `value` on
an input, name the type the way you already do with `querySelector`:

```ts
const inputs = document.querySelectorAll<HTMLInputElement>('input[type="text"]');
```

## Give the selector string a name {#sec-selectors-const}

A selector string is knowledge about your HTML. Rename a class in
`index.html`, and every copy of that string is suddenly wrong. In TypeScript
you can keep the string in one place:

```ts
const HIGHLIGHTED = '.highlight';

const count = document.querySelectorAll(HIGHLIGHTED).length;
```

The rename is one edit now. Look closely at what is stored there: the string,
not the elements the call found. Whether you may store the elements once and
keep using them later is exactly what the research box asks.

::: {.research title="What does `querySelectorAll` hand back?"}
The exercise below counts elements and loops over them. It also builds one
comma-separated line out of a collection. You have seen the call and one loop,
and the book stops explaining here.

1. `document.querySelectorAll('p')` does not return an array. What does it
   return, and what is that thing called?
2. Name two different ways to loop over the result.
3. Your program adds a new `<p>` to the page after the call. Does the result
   you stored earlier contain that new paragraph? Which word does MDN use for
   this behavior?
4. Array methods such as `map` and `filter` are missing from the result. How
   do you turn it into a real array?

In the exam you have the course material but no internet and no AI, so
looping over the result and knowing whether it updates itself should come
without looking anything up.
:::

## Exercise: the class blog {#sec-selectors-exercise}

{{< exercise blog-selectors >}}

Open `index.html` and read it once. There are three articles. Each one has a
heading, three paragraphs inside a `div` with the class `post`, a list of
tags, and a line of sources. Four buttons sit above the articles and do
nothing yet. `src/styles.css` already styles the page and ends with six
comments, one per task of part A.

## Part A: style the blog {#sec-selectors-css}

First open `src/index.ts`, delete what is in it, and put
`import './styles.css';` there, the same line the to-do list started with.
Without it the page never loads the stylesheet, and none of your rules shows
up. Then work in `src/styles.css` and replace each comment with a rule.
Every task needs one of the selector kinds from this chapter, and no task
needs a new class in `index.html`. Run `npm start` and keep the page open
while you work.

1. Give every heading inside an article the color `#1d3557`. The three post
   titles turn dark blue, and the "Class blog" heading at the top keeps its
   color.
2. Give every highlighted paragraph the background color `#fff3b0`. One
   paragraph in each article gets a yellow band.
3. Give the first paragraph of every post the font size `1.15rem`. Only the
   paragraph directly under each heading grows.
4. Give every odd tag the background color `#d8e2dc`. In each tag list the
   first and the third tag change, the middle one does not.
5. Give every link that points to another website the color `#b5179e`. The
   three MDN links change, and the links to `/notes/...` and `/imprint.html`
   stay as they are.
6. Give a tag under the mouse pointer the background color `#ffb703`. Move the
   pointer along a tag list and watch them light up one by one.

## Part B: count and change from TypeScript {#sec-selectors-typescript}

Back in `src/index.ts`, below the import, wire up the four buttons one at
a time. Reload the page after each step and try the button you just wrote.

1. **Count highlights.** When `#countButton` is clicked, count the paragraphs
   with the class `highlight` and write the number into the paragraph
   `#status`, for example `3 highlighted paragraphs`. Right after loading the
   page the answer is 3.
2. **Toggle highlights.** When `#toggleButton` is clicked, flip the class
   `highlight` on every paragraph inside an article. The first click takes the
   yellow away from three paragraphs and gives it to the other nine. The
   paragraph under the page heading and the `#status` paragraph never change,
   because neither of them sits inside an article.
3. Click "Count highlights" again. It has to say 9 now. If your program still
   says 3, read question 3 of the research box again and look at where you
   call `querySelectorAll`.
4. **Shout.** When `#shoutButton` is clicked, turn the text of every article
   heading into upper case with a loop.
5. **List tags.** When `#tagsButton` is clicked, write the text of all nine
   tags into `#status`, separated by a comma and a space:
   `html, vite, starter, css, colors, teamwork, debugging, devtools, html`.
   Do this one without writing a loop. Turn the collection into a real array
   first, as you found out in question 4 of the research box. Then `map`
   builds an array of the texts, and `join(', ')` glues that array into one
   string.

Finish with `npm run check`. Biome formats your file and reports anything it
does not like.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Name your selector strings

Put each selector string into a `const` at the top of the file and use the
name inside the handler. When you rename a class in `index.html` later, your
TypeScript has one line to fix.
:::
